title: SYSK Selects: How the Electoral College Works
summary: Josh Clark introduces this SYSK Selects rerun of the Electoral College episode, timed ahead of the 2020 election. The hosts explain how the system works: electors equal to each state's House and Senate seats (538 total, with three for D.C. under the 23rd Amendment), who are chosen by state parties and not always named on the ballot, and who meet in December to cast votes that are certified and read in Congress. They cover winner-take-all versus the district system in Maine and Nebraska, faithless electors, eligibility rules, and historical close or disputed elections: 1824 (John Quincy Adams and Andrew Jackson), 1876 (Hayes and Tilden), 1888 (Harrison and Cleveland), 2000 (Bush and Gore, Florida recount, Gore certifying his own defeat), and the 1800 Jefferson-Burr tie. They discuss reform proposals, polling on the system, and voter access concerns in Ohio. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Jack Mead in England and a sign-off urging people to vote.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and urges listeners to vote. The hosts joke about the election timing and admit they were surprised by how the Electoral College works, especially that voters are really choosing electors.

segments.title: Origins, electors and the compromise
segments.summary: The hosts explain the founders' distrust of direct popular vote and of Congress choosing the president, leading to the Electoral College compromise. Each state gets electors equal to its Senate and House seats, 538 total, with three for D.C. under the 23rd Amendment. Electors are not always on the ballot, and the hosts discuss how their identities are public.

segments.title: Faithless electors and who qualifies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss faithless electors and why electors are typically loyal party members. They cover the lack of strict constitutional qualifications, nomination by state parties, the bar on those engaged in insurrection or rebellion, and how a third-party candidate's electors are chosen.

segments.title: Winner-take-all versus district systems
segments.summary: Most states use winner-take-all, where the statewide popular vote winner gets all that state's electoral votes. Maine and Nebraska use a district system, giving two votes to the statewide winner and one per congressional district. The hosts note that split results have theoretically been possible but have not happened.

segments.title: Historical close elections: 1824, 1876, 1888
segments.summary: The hosts cover elections where the winner did not win the popular vote: 1824 (John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson, decided by the House under the Twelfth Amendment), 1876 (Hayes over Tilden, with Colorado's disputed votes), and 1888 (Cleveland won the popular vote but lost the electoral vote to Benjamin Harrison, with the South voting as a bloc).

segments.title: 2000 election and the Florida recount
segments.summary: The hosts recount the 2000 Bush-Gore election, which hinged on Florida. Issues included hanging chads, lost votes in one county, a limited recount, and disenfranchisement claims. Bush won Florida by a margin the hosts describe as under a few hundred votes, and winner-take-all gave him the state's electoral votes. Gore, as vice president and president of the Senate, had to read his own defeated electoral votes.

segments.title: Reform, polls and voter access
segments.summary: The hosts discuss arguments for and against the system, including effects on turnout and the states' weight by population. They note over 700 reform proposals, polling by the American Bar Association and political scientists, and public opinion polls from 1967 and 1981. They also raise concerns about Ohio's reduced early voting hours in Democratic counties. They close with the 1800 Jefferson-Burr tie and a call to vote.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jack Mead
segments.summary: Listener Jack Mead from England praises the show and asks for a support group for fans experiencing withdrawal between episodes. He also suggests a special episode with the hosts' wives.
